In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effect of PIs on the risk of developing osteoporosis and on the progression of bone loss in HIV-infected patients.
the development of new methods of treatment for the prevention and reversal of bone loss and osteoporosis.
the study of the effects of antiretroviral therapy on bone mineral density (BMD) in HIV-infected patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of PDE5 inhibitors is safe in patients with HIV infection and that the risk of developing HIV resistance is low.
the use of PIs in HIV-infected patients may lead to a high risk of bone loss, with the consequent high probability of progression to low bone mass or osteoporosis.
the risk of osteoporotic fracture and bone loss in HIV-infected patients is increased, especially in patients on PI therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have identified a number of novel genes associated with HIV infection and HIV-associated diseases, including HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND), HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN), and Kaposi sarcoma.

the risk of osteoporosis in HIV-infected patients is high, and that this risk is further exacerbated by PIs.

the risk of developing osteoporosis is high in HIV-infected patients and that this risk is increased in those who are treated with protease inhibitors (PIs) and in those with low CD4 counts.
we have a better understanding of how to treat people with HIV, and that we can do it in a safe and effective way.
